candidates.quote: In the middle of winter I at last discovered that there was in me an invincible summer.
candidates.author: Albert Camus
candidates.locator: the closing sentence of the first section, before the section break; in The Myth of Sisyphus and Other Essays (Knopf, 1955)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The winter month’s own promise, found in the author’s middle age and not his youth: the summer was in him all along.

candidates.translator: Neville Plaice, Stephen Plaice and Paul Knight, 1986
candidates.quote: True genesis is not at the beginning but at the end.
candidates.author: Ernst Bloch
candidates.locator: vol. III, ch. 55, Karl Marx and Humanity; Stuff of Hope, the closing paragraph of the book, pp. 1375 to 1376 (MIT Press); the opening clause of its third-last sentence
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last page of the longest book ever written about hope says the real beginning still lies ahead, which is the blurb of this month in one line.

candidates.quote: Whither, then, do the wings of the gate open? Thou knowest it not? INTO LIFE.
candidates.author: Franz Rosenzweig
candidates.locator: Part III, the closing section Gate, the last three sentences of the book (Holt, Rinehart and Winston, from the second German edition of 1930)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A book that opens on the words from death closes by sending its reader out of the door into life, which is exactly what a morning page should do.

candidates.quote: Thus our happiness will never consist (and it is right that it should not consist) in complete enjoyment, which would leave nothing more to be desired and would make our mind stupid; but it must consist in a perpetual progress to new pleasures and new perfections.
candidates.author: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
candidates.work: The Principles of Nature and of Grace, Founded on Reason
candidates.locator: section 18, the closing sentence, in The Monadology and Other Philosophical Writings (Clarendon Press, 1898), p. 424; Latta’s bracketed gloss [esprit] after mind is omitted
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last sentence of the treatise refuses a finished happiness and promises instead that there is always more to come, a year-end that is not an ending.

candidates.quote: From these pages I hope at least the following will endure: my trust in the people, and my faith in men and in the creation of a world in which it will be easier to love.
candidates.author: Paulo Freire
candidates.locator: Preface, the closing paragraph before the acknowledgements (Herder and Herder, 1970)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A teacher’s hope stated as the one thing he wants to outlast the book: a world in which it will be easier to love.

candidates.quote: The academy is not paradise. But learning is a place where paradise can be created. The classroom, with all its limitations, remains a location of possibility.
candidates.author: bell hooks
candidates.work: Teaching to Transgress: Education as the Practice of Freedom
candidates.locator: ch. 14, Ecstasy: Teaching and Learning Without Limits, the closing paragraph of the book, p. 207 (Routledge, 1994)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The book’s last paragraph admits the limits and still names the room a place of possibility, a closing line that opens a door.

candidates.quote: My most honored ladies, may God be praised, for now our City is entirely finished and completed, where all of you who love glory, virtue, and praise may be lodged in great honor, ladies from the past as well as from the present and future, for it has been built and established for every honorable lady.
candidates.author: Christine de Pizan
candidates.work: The Book of the City of Ladies
candidates.locator: Part III, ch. 19, The End of the Book: Christine Addresses the Ladies, III.19.1, the opening sentence (Persea, 1982)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last chapter hands over a finished city and opens its gates to women not yet born, which is the promise the books keep.

candidates.quote: In the beginning, woman was truly the sun. An authentic person.
candidates.author: Hiratsuka Raichō
candidates.work: In the Beginning, Woman Was the Sun (the manifesto of Seitō)
candidates.locator: Seitō, vol. 1, no. 1 (September 1911), the opening sentences; in In the Beginning, Woman Was the Sun: The Autobiography of a Japanese Feminist (Columbia University Press, 2006)
candidates.whyThisMonth: In the month the sun turns back, the most famous opening in Japanese feminism remembers a light that can be recovered.

candidates.quote: Hope is definitely not the same thing as optimism. It is not the conviction that something will turn out well, but the certainty that something makes sense, regardless of how it turns out.
candidates.author: Václav Havel
candidates.work: Disturbing the Peace: A Conversation with Karel Hvížďala
candidates.locator: ch. 5, The Politics of Hope (Alfred A. Knopf, 1990)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written by a man the state had jailed and would jail again, it gives the month a hope that does not depend on good news.

candidates.quote: Our life is an apprenticeship to the truth, that around every circle another can be drawn; that there is no end in nature, but every end is a beginning; that there is always another dawn risen on mid-noon, and under every deep a lower deep opens.
candidates.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
candidates.locator: Essays (First Series), Essay X, the second paragraph, p. 249 (James Munroe, 1841)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Every end is a beginning is the whole of December’s theme, said in the essay that is about nothing else.

candidates.quote: Hope means hoping when things are hopeless, or it is no virtue at all.
candidates.author: G. K. Chesterton
candidates.locator: ch. XII, Paganism and Mr. Lowes Dickinson (John Lane, 1905)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A short, cheerful definition for a dark morning: hope is for the days that do not seem to deserve it.

candidates.quote: Hence, given the right nourishment there is nothing that will not grow, and deprived of it there is nothing that will not wither away.
candidates.author: Mencius
candidates.locator: Book VI, Part A, 8, the Ox Mountain passage
candidates.whyThisMonth: The stripped hillside that keeps putting out new shoots is the oldest renewal parable in the year, and it ends on what nourishment can do.

candidates.quote: A beginner must look upon himself as making a garden, wherein our Lord may take His delight, but in a soil unfruitful, and abounding in weeds. His Majesty roots up the weeds, and has to plant good herbs.
candidates.author: Teresa of Ávila
candidates.work: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus
candidates.locator: ch. XI, section 10, the opening of the four waters (third edition, ed. Benedict Zimmerman, Thomas Baker, 1904)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It lets the reader begin again as a beginner, in poor ground, with the weeding already promised.

candidates.quote: For women, then, poetry is not a luxury. It is a vital necessity of our existence. It forms the quality of the light within which we predicate our hopes and dreams toward survival and change, first made into language, then into idea, then into more tangible action.
candidates.author: Audre Lorde
candidates.locator: Chrysalis, no. 3 (1977); Sister Outsider (Crossing Press, 1984), p. 37
candidates.whyThisMonth: It traces how a hope becomes a word, then an idea, then a deed, which is the path a December resolution has to take.

candidates.quote: We also have our dream of a Garden: but it lies in a distant future. We dream that woman shall eat of the tree of knowledge together with man, and that side by side and hand close to hand, through ages of much toil and labour, they shall together raise about them an Eden nobler than any the Chaldean dreamed of; an Eden created by their own labour and made beautiful by their own fellowship.
candidates.author: Olive Schreiner
candidates.locator: ch. VI, Certain Objections, the closing pages (T. Fisher Unwin, 1911)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The book’s close turns Eden around, from a garden lost behind us to one still to be made, a closing that opens forward.

candidates.quote: A true conception of the relation of the sexes will not admit of conqueror and conquered; it knows of but one great thing: to give of one’s self boundlessly, in order to find one’s self richer, deeper, better. That alone can fill the emptiness, and transform the tragedy of woman’s emancipation into joy, limitless joy.
candidates.author: Emma Goldman
candidates.locator: the closing sentences, in Anarchism and Other Essays (Mother Earth Publishing Association, 1910)
candidates.whyThisMonth: An essay titled for a tragedy ends in limitless joy, the turn this month asks every closing line to make.
